items.title: Wendell Brunious interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: And then I heard some record, I think it was “Somebody Stole My Gal,” and Bix plays this real nice phrase, and he went down to this kind of unusual note that rubbed up against the root of the chord.

ctx.x: Well I mean, but it’s like you know that’s really maturing type of tactics and things to do that help you to mature faster. I think so.

I do too. I didn’t know anything about improvising when I first heard these jazz records. I didn’t know they were making it up out of their heads. I just liked the music, you know. And then I remember hearing a Bix Beiderbecke record and reading all the critics or the writers you know they say the same thing. I think one guy reads something and then he recycles it you know. But everything I read about Bix Beiderbecke, they said he was fond of ninths and thirteenths. I thought oh well, that’s nice. And then the…

eight, nine. Oh, that’s a ninth. Oh that’s a ninth. Oh, yeah. You know, light — 20 watt light bulb. Oh that’s what a ninth is. And I went nine, ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen, oh, that’s a thirteenth. Oh, yeah, I’ve heard him do that. And then of course, as I mentioned, when I first heard Charlie Parker and I go back to my Dixieland band and try and play like Charlie Parker. Well then every solo I played, I went immediately for the ninth. Ninth, ninth, ninth — Banjo players, “Aw, Dan.” MR: I don’t want to rush you…
